title: One Workload to Rule Them All: Workload Aware Scheduling for Distributed AI Training on Kubernetes
tldr: Kubernetes now has Workload, PodGroup and composite PodGroup APIs so kube-scheduler can gang-schedule, preempt and place a whole distributed job instead of single pods. Kubeflow Trainer builds these into TrainJob runtimes so platform admins set gang and topology rules while scientists only write a training function.

key_points.text: Pod-by-pod scheduling deadlocks distributed jobs: two 8-GPU jobs on three 4-GPU nodes can each grab part of the capacity and neither starts.
Other gaps: preempting one pod leaves the rest of the gang idle, launcher and worker roles are scheduled as unrelated pods, and placement ignores racks, slowing gradient sync.
Kueue, KAI, Volcano, YuniKorn and the scheduler-plugins project all tackled gang scheduling; a new working group, started about a year ago at KubeCon Japan, aims for one common API.

A PodGroup carries a scheduling policy (gang with a minimum count), topology constraints, a disruption mode and shared resource claims; the scheduler checks the whole group against a cluster snapshot before admitting it.
Preemption has two modes upstream: single (evict one pod) and all (evict the whole pod group).
Composite pod groups express hierarchy with a minimum group count, useful for multi-layer jobs and disaggregated prefill/decode inference.
Kubeflow Trainer splits personas: admins define runtimes with zone/block/rack levels of scheduling policy; scientists call a Python SDK; JobSet and LeaderWorkerSet run underneath.
The same scheduling fields are meant to appear in TrainJob, JobSet and LeaderWorkerSet so users get one experience across workload types.

Kind demo: without gang scheduling a 5-pod job ran 4 pods and blocked a smaller job; with a gang policy the big job waited, the small one ran, and events named the unmet min count. A rack constraint kept each job in one rack.
TrainJob can report progress and ETA from framework callbacks; the speaker proposes using it for backfill and for preempting jobs that will finish later.
Kueue stays on top for quotas, cluster queues and multi-cluster; its topology-aware scheduling overlaps with the new upstream work and the two are being aligned.

numbers.text: Workload and PodGroup APIs are beta in Kubernetes 1.37; composite pod groups are alpha with beta expected in 1.38 and GA hoped for 1.40.
Trainer integration with composite pod groups is planned for Trainer 2.5, about two months out.
Demo cluster: 4 nodes across 2 racks; the first job asked for 5 pods.

open_gaps.text: Deep topology across multiple composite pod groups is slow for kube-scheduler; performance work is ongoing so 1,000 pods do not take an hour to schedule.
How Kueue's topology-aware scheduling hands off to the scheduler's own version is still being worked out, so the two will overlap for a while.
Topology is label-based only; health-aware topology (hardware degraded by heat or cooling failures) is an open issue.
Volcano maintainers are not yet engaged in the API design; the speaker asked them to join.

opportunities.text: Try the beta Workload and PodGroup APIs on a kind cluster with a gang policy and a rack constraint, as in the demo.
Bring Volcano or other scheduler use cases to the workload-aware scheduling working group and Trainer calls.
Prototype backfill or ETA-aware preemption using TrainJob's reported progress and ETA.
Adopt the shared scheduling fields in your own workload controller so it composes pod groups like TrainJob and JobSet.
